content_units: A one-day marathon on   identity and memory   works best when it moves from fractured selfhood to collective remembrance, ending on a note that feels expansive rather than punishing. This lineup spans six countries/eras/styles and stays under the time cap while creating a clear emotional arc: confusion, reconstruction, longing, reinvention, erasure, and finally communal memory.
Film   Runtime   Content note level   Why it belongs here
Persona  (Sweden, 1966)   83 min     Medium     A bracing overture about identity splitting, projection, and the instability of the self; it sharpens the audience’s attention from the first frame.
Memento  (USA, 2000)   113 min     High     Moves from psychological fracture into memory as a survival mechanism, showing how identity can be built from unreliable fragments.
After Life  (Japan, 1998)   118 min     Low     A tonal reset after two intense films; gentle, humane, and literal about memory selection, asking what single remembrance defines a life.

The Double Life of Veronique  (France/Poland, 1991)   98 min     Low-Medium     Deepens the program from memory as record to identity as intuition, resemblance, and felt inheritance across borders and selves.

Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind  (USA, 2004)   108 min     Medium     Places love and selfhood at the center, asking whether erasing pain also erases the version of ourselves formed through intimacy.

Waltz with Bashir  (Israel, 2008)   90 min     High     Ends the marathon by widening from personal memory to historical memory, showing how forgetting can be both psychological defense and moral crisis.

-   Placement logic:   After  Persona  destabilizes the self,  Memento  asks what remains when memory itself cannot hold. Its reverse structure turns viewers into participants, forcing them to experience confusion as method rather than theme.

5)  Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind

-   Placement logic:   By this point the audience has considered memory philosophically; this film makes it intimate. It asks whether grief, embarrassment, and heartbreak are damage to be removed or necessary evidence of who we have been.

-   Placement logic:   The finale expands the day from private identity to public history. It is the right closing work because it insists that memory is not only personal texture but ethical responsibility, and that what is repressed can return with devastating force.
Opening Keynote: Before the First Screening

Welcome to   Identity and Memory  , a marathon built around one of cinema’s oldest and deepest questions: if our memories shift, fail, or are rewritten, who exactly are we? Across today’s six films, memory appears as wound, archive, fantasy, burden, and grace. Some of these characters cling to the past in order to survive; others try to escape it; still others discover that memory is never entirely private, because history, desire, and other people live inside it.

The sequence is designed as a progression rather than a survey. We begin with fractured selves and unreliable perception, move through acts of recollection and chosen remembrance, and end in the territory where personal forgetting meets collective responsibility. By the end of the day, I hope the question will no longer be simply “What do we remember?” but “What kind of person—or society—do our memories allow us to become?”
Closing Keynote: After the Final Film

What today’s lineup reveals is that identity is never fixed and memory is never neutral. We saw characters assemble themselves from scraps, protect themselves through forgetting, and discover that even erased or inaccessible memories continue shaping desire, guilt, love, and action. Cinema is uniquely suited to this theme because it mirrors memory itself: fragments, flashes, loops, distortions, and sudden returns.

Taken together, these six films suggest that to remember is not merely to retrieve the past but to interpret it—and that interpretation carries emotional and ethical weight. We leave the marathon with no simple answer, only a richer tension: memory can imprison, but it can also humanize; identity can fracture, but it can also be remade. If the day has done its work, we walk out not with certainty about who we are, but with greater tenderness toward how precariously, and how creatively, a self is held together.
To stay under the 13-hour limit, this schedule assumes:
- no pre-show trailers or extended introductions
- a short closing keynote after the final screening
- content note levels interpreted broadly as   Low / Medium / High   for intensity, distressing themes, violence, and psychological pressure
